metronidazole.name: Metronidazole
metronidazole.summary: An antibiotic used for bacterial infections of the skin, mouth and gums, and the vagina and pelvis, and the usual treatment for trichomoniasis. It comes as tablets, liquid, suppositories, gels and creams, and the NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days afterwards.
usedFor: Mouth infections, including infected gums and dental abscesses
Bacterial vaginosis and pelvic inflammatory disease
Infected insect bites, skin ulcers, bed sores and wounds
Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection, which the NHS says is usually treated with metronidazole
metronidazole.howItWorks: Metronidazole stops the growth of the bacteria or parasites that cause an infection. Laboratory studies describe it as being switched on inside susceptible organisms, many of which live without oxygen, by pathways that human cells do not have. Once switched on, it forms short-lived chemical products that bind to DNA and damage it.
metronidazole.onset: The NHS says most infections start to improve within a few days, although the full course is still finished.

regimenNote: Available as tablets, liquid, suppositories, skin gel and cream, vaginal gel, and as an injection given in hospital.

sections.heading: What is metronidazole used for?
sections.body: Metronidazole is an antibiotic that the NHS describes as treating several bacterial infections. These include infections of the skin, rosacea, infections of the mouth such as infected gums and dental abscesses, bacterial vaginosis and pelvic inflammatory disease. It can also be used for infected insect bites, skin ulcers, bed sores and wounds. Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection, is treated with antibiotics, usually metronidazole. The form prescribed depends on the infection and how serious it is. It comes as tablets, a liquid to drink, suppositories, skin gel, skin cream and vaginal gel. It can also be given by injection, but this is usually done only in hospital. For most infections, the NHS says people feel better within a few days.

sections.heading: How does metronidazole work?
sections.body: Metronidazole stops the growth of the bacteria or parasites that cause an infection. It belongs to a group of medicines called nitroimidazoles, which also includes tinidazole. Laboratory studies describe it as being switched on inside susceptible organisms, many of which live without oxygen. The switching-on pathways are absent in the aerobic cells of the human body, which helps explain why the medicine targets microbes. Once switched on, it forms short-lived products that bind to DNA and cause damage, including breaks in the DNA strands. Metronidazole is active against parasites such as Giardia and Trichomonas vaginalis and against anaerobic bacteria such as Bacteroides and Clostridium species. Tinidazole is described as similar to metronidazole in its range of activity and side effects.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body: The NHS lists feeling or being sick, diarrhoea and a slight metallic taste in the mouth as common side effects of the tablets, liquid, suppositories and vaginal gel. A hospital leaflet also lists stomach cramps, headache and dizziness, and notes that drowsiness can occur. Thrush is a possible side effect, most often with the vaginal gel. Serious side effects are rare and, according to the NHS, affect fewer than 1 in 1,000 people. Yellow skin or eyes, which the NHS links with liver or gallbladder problems, needs prompt contact with the GP or NHS 111. A headache with a high temperature and stiff neck, together with tiredness and eyes sensitive to bright light, or with seeing or hearing things that are not there, confusion or trouble speaking, is an emergency: call 999 or go to A&E. Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, can signal a serious allergic reaction and also needs a 999 call. A hospital factsheet adds that numbness or tingling in the hands and feet can occur with longer courses, a reason to speak to the prescriber.

sections.heading: Metronidazole and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS advises not drinking alcohol while taking metronidazole tablets or liquid or using suppositories. It says to keep avoiding alcohol for 2 days after treatment finishes. The reason is that alcohol with metronidazole can cause feeling or being sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, a fast or pounding heartbeat (palpitations) and headache. The NHS also lists feeling unable to stop drinking alcohol during treatment among the reasons to talk to a doctor before using it. Skin creams and gels carry a much lower risk, because little of the medicine is absorbed. MedlinePlus, a US source, gives a longer wait of at least 3 days after the last dose, so advice differs between publishers.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care?
sections.body: The NHS page on who can take metronidazole mentions people who have ever had an allergic reaction to it or another medicine, people who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and people who are having blood tests. Liver problems, dialysis and diseases of the nervous system are further points to tell the prescriber about for tablets, liquid or suppositories. On pregnancy, the NHS says metronidazole may be an option but advises discussing it with a doctor first. It also says there is no evidence of an effect on fertility in men or women. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says usual courses can be used during breastfeeding, with the baby watched for poor feeding, stomach upset or oral thrush. UK package leaflets are more cautious about tablets in pregnancy, so the prescriber weighs each situation. The NHS says metronidazole does not stop contraception working, though vomiting or severe or prolonged diarrhoea may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk during metronidazole treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days after finishing. Alcohol with metronidazole can cause feeling or being sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, a pounding heartbeat and headache.

faqs.q: Does metronidazole stop the contraceptive pill working?
faqs.a: The NHS says metronidazole does not stop any type of contraception working. If it causes vomiting or severe or prolonged diarrhoea, contraceptive pills may not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can metronidazole be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it may be possible to use it in pregnancy but advises discussing it with a doctor first. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says usual courses can be used while breastfeeding, with the baby watched for feeding problems.
The NHS says metronidazole usually does not affect driving or cycling. A hospital leaflet notes that it can cause drowsiness and dizziness, so some people may feel unfit to drive.
The NHS says people usually feel better within a few days for most infections. The full course is still finished as prescribed even when symptoms ease.

nitroimidazoles.name: Nitroimidazoles
nitroimidazoles.summary: Antibiotic and antiparasitic medicines, including metronidazole and tinidazole, that act on susceptible bacteria and parasites that live without oxygen.
nitroimidazoles.mechanism: Nitroimidazoles are switched on inside susceptible organisms by pathways that are absent in aerobic human cells. The switched-on form produces short-lived products that bind to DNA and damage it. In Giardia, enzymes such as pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase help to switch on 5-nitroimidazoles including metronidazole and tinidazole.
cautions: For metronidazole, the NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days afterwards.
Tinidazole is described as similar to metronidazole in its range of activity and side effects, so similar cautions may apply.
classEffects: Feeling sick, diarrhoea and a metallic taste are the common side effects of metronidazole.
